summary: Japan's southernmost national park, in the Yaeyama Islands. Iriomote is almost all jungle, mangrove and river, home to the Iriomote cat and part of a World Heritage Site; between it and Ishigaki lies Sekisei Lagoon, Japan's largest coral reef. Take a boat up the Urauchi River to Mariyudu Falls, snorkel at Kabira Bay or Shiraho, and walk the stone-walled lanes of Taketomi.
story: The Yaeyama Islands are the far south-western end of Japan. Iriomote, the largest, is steep, wet and covered almost entirely by subtropical evergreen forest, cut by rivers such as the Urauchi, the longest in Okinawa Prefecture, and the Nakama, whose banks hold Japan's largest mangrove forest. Ishigaki, the busy hub, has Okinawa's highest mountain, Omotodake, and the wetlands of Nagura Amparu. Between the two islands lies Sekisei Lagoon, the largest coral reef in Japan, with more than 360 species of coral.

Iriomote's forests are the only home of the Iriomote cat, a small wild cat of which only about a hundred survive. The crested serpent eagle hunts over the forest edge, Ryukyu wild boar root in the valleys, and the Yaeyama palm grows wild only on Iriomote and Ishigaki. On the reef, manta rays and sea turtles feed, and at Shiraho on Ishigaki grows a huge colony of blue coral.

People have long farmed and fished on these islands; on Taketomi a whole village of red-tiled, stone-walled houses survives, and festivals such as Iriomote's Shichi, a national Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property, still mark the farming year. Iriomote itself was mined for coal from 1886 until 1960. Today Ishigaki is the islands' busy hub, with an airport and ferries to the other islands, while Iriomote has no airstrip and its road runs only along the coast.

The Ryukyu government made Iriomote a government park in April 1972, and on 15 May that year, when Okinawa returned to Japan, it became Iriomote National Park. Ishigaki and its seas were added in 2007 and the park renamed Iriomote-Ishigaki; the marine park zones were greatly enlarged in 2012, and in 2016 the park was extended over almost the whole of Iriomote. In July 2021 Iriomote was inscribed as part of a natural World Heritage Site with Amami Ōshima, Tokunoshima and northern Okinawa.
howItWorks: Iriomote-Ishigaki is a regional park in which most land, about 62 per cent, is state-owned. The villages, farms and harbours of Iriomote, Ishigaki and the small islands of Taketomi, Kohama, Kuroshima, Hatoma and Hateruma lie within or beside it, in the city of Ishigaki and the town of Taketomi.

About 13 per cent of the land is special protection zone and about 71 per cent special zone, much of it Class 1, covering the heart of Iriomote. At sea, more than twenty marine park zones protect Sekisei Lagoon and the reefs around the islands; together they are the largest area of marine park in Japan, and collecting designated corals, fish and shellfish there needs permission. Motorised traffic is restricted in parts of the Urauchi and Nakama river basins.

On Iriomote, numbers are now limited by law at the most popular wild places. Under the national Ecotourism Promotion Act, Taketomi town has, since March 2025, restricted entry to five places it designated as specific natural tourism resources — the Hinai River, which leads to Pinaisara Falls, the Nishida River, Komidake, the upper Urauchi River and Tedōzan — each with a daily cap on visitors, from 30 to 200 people. Entry needs the town's approval in advance and an approval fee, and visitors must go with a registered guide (at Komidake, the upper Urauchi and Tedōzan, the town's training course is an alternative); entering without approval is an offence. Check with Taketomi town before you go.

sights.name: Urauchi River and Mariyudu Falls (浦内川・マリユドゥの滝)
sights.note: Take a boat up Okinawa's longest river through mangrove and jungle, then walk to the broad, stepped falls of Mariyudu and on to Kanpire.

sights.name: Pinaisara Falls (ピナイサーラの滝)
sights.note: At 55 metres the tallest waterfall in Okinawa Prefecture, reached by kayak and trail up the Hinai River — a capped, permit-only route.

sights.name: Nakama River (仲間川)
sights.note: Sightseeing boats run up through Japan's largest mangrove forest to a giant sakishima-suō tree.

sights.name: Hoshizuna-no-hama (星砂の浜)
sights.note: A beach on Iriomote's north coast whose 'star sand' is the shells of tiny marine organisms.

sights.name: Kabira Bay (川平湾)
sights.note: A bay of white sand, islets and luminous water on Ishigaki's north coast; see the coral from a glass-bottomed boat.

sights.name: Cape Hirakubo (平久保崎)
sights.note: Ishigaki's northern tip, with a lighthouse and views over reefs and open sea.

sights.name: Shiraho (白保)
sights.note: A reef on Ishigaki's east coast famous for its huge blue coral colony; snorkel or take a glass-bottomed boat.

sights.name: Nagura Amparu (名蔵アンパル)
sights.note: Mangroves and tidal flats on Ishigaki's west coast, a Ramsar site and a stopping place for migrating birds.

sights.name: Iriomote Wildlife Conservation Center (西表野生生物保護センター)
sights.note: The Ministry of the Environment's centre at Komi on Iriomote: the Iriomote cat, its protection and the island's wildlife.

sights.name: Taketomi Island Visitor Center Yugafukan (竹富島ビジターセンター ゆがふ館)
sights.note: Taketomi's island culture, village and reefs.

entrances: New Ishigaki Airport, with flights from Tokyo, Osaka and Naha
Ishigaki Port, the hub for ferries to Iriomote, Taketomi, Kohama, Kuroshima, Hatoma and Hateruma
Uehara Port and Ōhara Port on Iriomote, linked by the island's coast-road bus
planYourVisit.reservations: Entry to the Hinai River (for Pinaisara Falls), the Nishida River, Komidake, the upper Urauchi River and Tedōzan on Iriomote is capped and needs approval from Taketomi town in advance, with a fee, usually through a registered guide. River boats, kayak tours and diving trips are best booked ahead, and ferries are often cancelled in rough seas. Check before you go.
permits: Hinai River (Pinaisara Falls) — approval from Taketomi town, 200 people a day
Nishida River — approval, 100 people a day
Upper Urauchi River — approval, 50 people a day
Komidake and Tedōzan — approval, 30 people a day each
lodging: Hotels and guesthouses in Ishigaki city and around the island
Inns and small resorts along Iriomote's coast road
Guesthouses on Taketomi, Kohama and the other small islands
seasonalClosures: Ferries and river boats stop in typhoons and rough seas, most often between July and October

weather: The Yaeyama Islands are subtropical and warm all year. Winters are mild but often windy and overcast, with seas that can cancel ferries. The rainy season comes early, from about May into June. Summer is hot, humid and bright, with fierce sun. Typhoons strike or pass close most years between July and October, stopping ferries and flights. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable times for walking; the sea is warm enough for snorkelling for much of the year.
directions: Flights from Tokyo, Osaka and other cities reach New Ishigaki Airport in about three to four hours, and frequent flights from Naha take about an hour. From the airport, buses run to Ishigaki Port in about 30 minutes. Ferries from Ishigaki Port reach Iriomote's Uehara and Ōhara ports, Taketomi, Kohama, Kuroshima and the other islands; services between the small islands are limited, so it is often easiest to return to Ishigaki between trips. On Iriomote, a bus runs along the coast road between Uehara and Ōhara four times a day, and cars can be hired. Taketomi is small enough to explore on foot or by bicycle.

chronology.text: Coal mining begins on Iriomote; it continues, with breaks, until 1960.
The Ryukyu government designates Iriomote a government park in April; on 15 May, with Okinawa's return to Japan, it becomes Iriomote National Park.
The first marine park zones are designated around Taketomi, Kuroshima, Aragusuku and Sekisei Lagoon.
Part of Ishigaki is added on 1 August and the park is renamed Iriomote-Ishigaki.
The marine park zones are greatly enlarged and Hatoma and Hateruma are added.
The park is extended over almost the whole of Iriomote.
Iriomote is inscribed as part of a natural World Heritage Site.
The Ministry of the Environment approves Iriomote's ecotourism plan, allowing visitor numbers to be capped at five sites.

The park is extended over Nagura Bay in March. In August Taketomi town sets daily limits on visitors to the Hinai and Nishida rivers, Komidake, the upper Urauchi and Tedōzan, in force from 1 March 2025.

safety: Rivers on Iriomote rise very fast after rain. Never cross a swollen river, and walk the interior only with a registered guide.
Box jellyfish (habu-kurage) occur in summer; swim inside stinger nets where provided, and leave the water if warned.
Currents over the reef edge and through channels are strong; snorkel in sheltered water or with a guide.
Drive slowly on Iriomote's roads, especially at night: Iriomote cats are killed by cars.
regulations: Entry to the five capped sites on Iriomote — Hinai River, Nishida River, Komidake, upper Urauchi and Tedōzan — requires Taketomi town's approval.
Do not feed, chase or photograph the Iriomote cat with flash; it is a special natural monument.
In the marine park zones, collecting designated corals, fish and shellfish needs permission; never stand on coral.
Motorised traffic is restricted in parts of the Urauchi and Nakama river basins.
